description:
We are a team of three software engineering students passionate about technology, AI, and space exploration. We have experience in Python, Java, JavaScript, Vue.js, and software development.

For NASA Space Apps 2026, we're developing astronaut health monitoring software using data analysis, visualization, and anomaly detection.
summary:
Houston Pulse is a health monitoring app we built for astronauts on long missions. On the ISS, if something looks off, the crew can talk to doctors on the ground almost right away. On the way to Mars that’s not true anymore: a message can take up to 22 minutes to reach Earth, and you can’t just fly a sick crew member home. So astronauts need to be able to read their own data and know when something actually needs attention.

The app shows each astronaut’s vitals (heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, sleep and mood) on a body map, with charts covering the whole mission. Data comes from simulated wearable devices or can be entered by hand. We compare each new value to the astronaut’s own baseline from the previous days, and flag it as “Watch” if it moves unusually far or keeps trending in one direction. “Critical” alerts only come from published medical thresholds (AHA, ADA, CDC), and the app always explains why something was flagged. When an alert is critical and the signal round trip to Earth is longer than 10 minutes, the app switches to an Earth-independent mode with next steps and a report ready to send to the flight surgeon.

It’s not a diagnosis tool. The goal is to help the crew notice changes early and know when to ask for help.
details:
What it does

On the way to Mars, a question to Mission Control takes up to 22 minutes to arrive, and the answer takes as long to come back. A crew exposed to NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight cannot wait for the ground to notice that something is drifting. It has to see it first.

Houston Pulse gives the crew that ability. It tracks six health indicators (heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep and mood), measures each astronaut against their own baseline, flags what changes, explains why in plain language, and says what to do next.

How it works

  1. Collect. Readings arrive from crew devices through a device API, or by manual entry. Every value passes plausibility checks before it is stored.
  2. Compare. A value outside a documented normal range, 2.5 standard deviations away from the baseline, or a significant trend in the direction that matters raises a Watch.
  3. Check. A Critical alert requires a documented emergency level from the American Heart Association, the American Diabetes Association or the CDC. No statistical rule can raise one on its own.
  4. Explain. Every alert states its reason, what the indicator measures, why it matters in space, and the next step.

The crew reads all of this on one screen. A vital ring shows one coloured arc per indicator (Nominal, Watch, Critical) around an interactive 3D holographic body. Flagged zones pulse; the heart beats at the latest measured rate. Click a zone to open its indicators, its history and its guidance. A daily checklist shows which measurements are due, and a report for the flight surgeon is one click away.

Earth-independent mode

The same alert does not call for the same response everywhere. In low Earth orbit, the flight surgeon is seconds away. In Mars transit, the round trip takes about 45 minutes.

When a Critical alert occurs and Earth cannot answer in time, Houston Pulse switches protocol: it guides the crew through onboard monitoring steps, sends a report to Earth, and counts down to the earliest possible reply. This applies NASA’s Earth-Independent Medical Operations (EIMO) concept to a working interface.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Earlier detection. The crew sees a change in its own health before it becomes an emergency.
  • Personal, not average. Each astronaut is their own reference, so a normal value for one person does not hide a drift in another.
  • Trust. Every alert is explained and sourced, so the crew understands it and can act on it.
  • Reach beyond space. The same approach serves isolated teams on Earth: polar stations, ships, remote communities.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLModel with SQLite, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, tested with pytest.
  • Frontend: Vue 3, TypeScript, Vite, Plotly for charts, Three.js for the 3D body, generated procedurally in code.
  • Devices: a device API that accepts readings today from simulated devices, and real wearables could connect through it.

How it is creative

  • Guidance that adapts to distance. The protocol changes with the signal delay of the mission, instead of always answering “call a doctor”.
  • A body you can read. The holographic figure and the vital ring turn six data streams into one picture the crew grasps at a glance.
  • Alerts that explain themselves. Each flag carries its reason and its source.
  • One tool, three environments. Low Earth orbit, lunar base and Mars transit, each with its own signal delay.

Factors we considered

  • Rigorous clinical guardrails. Every Critical threshold is traceable to a published medical reference. The tool gives monitoring steps only; diagnosis and treatment stay with the flight surgeon and the Crew Medical Officer.
  • Transparent data. All crew data and devices in this prototype are simulated, and the interface labels them as such on every screen.
  • Usability under stress. Plain language, colour plus text for every status, full keyboard access.
  • Known limit, next step. Our thresholds are established adult references. In flight, resting core temperature rises by about 1 °C (Stahn et al., 2017). The next version will make thresholds follow that expected in-flight curve, a space-adapted baseline.
